A listener workflow living in the tap or bucket does the manifest work with each ecosystem's own tooling; the generated project ships a reference listener and setup guide under docs/packaging/ as a copy-into-your-tap bundle, not code it runs. The jobs are gated on a fine-grained PAT with Contents-write on the target repository only, skip with a visible warning when the secret is unset, run with no workflow permissions of their own, and never join the check gate.

Reason: generating a formula, cask or manifest in every producing project duplicates sha256 computation, PyPI resource resolution, per-OS asset matching and each ecosystem's audit rules — and their bugs — once per generated project. Dispatching keeps that logic in one downstream place, written with the tools the ecosystems maintain for exactly this job. The jobs live in release.yml because a release event fired by the workflow token cannot trigger another workflow. The listener opens its own PR with its own token, so the PAT needs no pull-request scope.

Rejected alternative: render and push the formula/manifest from the generated project — the original design of this record, replaced for the duplication above.

Rejected alternative: one shared enum or parent toggle — an owner may want one ecosystem only.

Consequence: binaries are single-architecture per OS; the Scoop PyPI fallback is best-effort because Scoop's tooling assumes binary downloads; the listener is not validated by this template's tests; payload validation is the listener's job.

docs.title: primary_executable is the single source for the distribution payload
docs.text:
Id: 40888b40-730c-4575-b68c-401b4eeccc06 Type: decision Status: active Evidence: confirmed Source: ADR-017 (docs/adr/017-opt-in-homebrew-scoop-distribution.md) Revisit when: a fourth executable architecture is added, or the launcher stops needing network access on first run See: standalone-executables.md#three-architecture-named-executable-toggles-instead-of-one-brand-toggle — d5aed1a0-0b7c-4ac3-9d75-fb9568d9e34d — as of 2026-10-11

A hidden computed variable picks freezer over compiler over launcher, or is empty when no executable toggle is on. Non-empty means a Homebrew cask and a Scoop binary manifest fed from the GitHub release; empty means a Homebrew formula built from the PyPI sdist and a Scoop pipx manifest.

Reason: PyInstaller and Nuitka produce fully self-contained binaries; the PyCrucible launcher still needs the network on first run, so it is the fallback of last resort. One computed variable mirrors the role primary_component plays for console-script precedence: no template re-spells the ordering inline.

Rejected alternative: re-derive the ordering per template — the drift primary_component already exists to prevent.

docs.title: Optional PyPI publishing
docs.text:
Id: 20be7463-ca95-4d01-82c9-71f632d1b4be Type: decision Status: active Evidence: confirmed Source: issue #382; maintainer decisions while implementing it, 2026-10-11; ADR-039 (docs/adr/039-optional-pypi-publishing.md) Revisit when: the PyPI project name becomes its own question, or Homebrew / Scoop gain a non-PyPI source for a pure-Python package See: release-automation.md#the-workflow_dispatch-trigger-on-releaseyml-stays-the-publish-environment-is-the-containment — 0d93a35d-46a3-4ac6-b072-fc07da789842 — as of 2026-10-11

include_pypi_publish is a boolean toggle, seeded on by every preset, so existing projects and copier update keep publishing. When it is off:

  • release.yml does not render pypi-publish, and drops it from the needs of attach-github-release and finalize-release. build still produces and attests the wheel and sdist, and attach-github-release still uploads them, so every release keeps its distributions.
  • build keeps the publish environment. It mints build-provenance attestations there, and the environment's main-only deployment-branch policy is what stops a workflow_dispatch run from another branch. So the setup guide drops only the PyPI publisher registration. The "Restrict the publish environment to main" step stays.
  • The README and installation.rst install from git+https://github.com/<user>/<repo> (uv tool install, uvx --from, uv add, pip install) and say the release assets carry the wheel and sdist. The README PyPI badges and its PyPI-based Analysis links are dropped. The PyPI publication-attestation text in installation.rst is dropped too, along with PyPI mentions in CONTRIBUTING.md, the repo-setup skill and the after-copy message.

Homebrew and Scoop. A Homebrew formula is built from the PyPI sdist, and the Scoop pipx manifest polls PyPI. Only a prebuilt executable (a cask or binary manifest) is fetched from the GitHub Release. A hidden can_distribute_natively (is_app and either PyPI publishing or a primary_executable) therefore gates include_homebrew and include_scoop. Without it they are not asked, and their default repeats the guard, so a preset cannot turn on a tap or bucket that could never update.

Rejected alternative: leave Homebrew/Scoop ungated and document the caveat. Rejected: it renders a tap/bucket dispatch whose formula or manifest can never resolve, which is a failure on first release that the template can prevent at question time.

Rejected alternative: point the install docs at a GitHub Release wheel download. Rejected in favor of Git URL installs, which work with every installer the docs already show, can be pinned with @<tag>, and work over SSH for private repositories.

Rejected alternative: make the PyPI project name its own question in this change. Deferred as a separate concern: it decouples the distribution name from the package name, which touches far more than the publish job.

Consequence: a project can release without PyPI, and that choice survives copier update. An explicit --data include_homebrew=true still renders the tap even when the question is gated off — Copier applies passed data to an unasked question, the existing contract of the is_app gate too. The template-ci litestar-kafka scenario renders with PyPI off so actionlint checks the web variant of finalize-release's needs without pypi-publish.

docs.title: Archetype presets name project shapes; library is the default
docs.text:
Id: a14ee38b-12ed-49c8-b452-12b330cf9d10 Type: decision Status: active Evidence: confirmed Source: ADR-016 (docs/adr/016-archetype-based-presets.md); the preset mechanism it reshapes came from PR #141; ADR-025 and ADR-039 for the two toggles every preset seeds Revisit when: a distinct service/worker archetype (worker + broker + database) proves common enough to be a fifth choice See: standalone-executables.md#three-architecture-named-executable-toggles-instead-of-one-brand-toggle — d5aed1a0-0b7c-4ac3-9d75-fb9568d9e34d — as of 2026-10-11

The preset question offers library (default; seeds examples), tool (cli, tui, pydantic_settings), web (web with FastAPI, pydantic_settings, postgres, redis) and full (everything). Every preset also seeds docs and pypi_publish on (ADR-025, ADR-039). A preset only seeds toggle defaults through the hidden preset_map; every toggle is still asked and stored. tool seeds none of the standalone-executable toggles, and web seeds neither worker, MCP nor the database UIs.

Reason: the earlier minimal/standard/full/custom ladder answered "how much tooling" while adopters think in shapes — a library, a PyPI-shipped CLI/TUI tool, a web app. standard was CLI-lite under a size name, nothing named the library shape, and custom existed only to keep --defaults output byte-identical when presets were introduced — meaningless once every preset is tunable. library is the default because an unattended run should produce the smallest, most conservative surface. tool is PyPI-first because the maintainer ships tools mostly via PyPI and freezes them only occasionally; one deliberate flip beats a default most tools would turn back off.

Rejected alternative: keep custom as a migration cushion — presets had shipped only days earlier, so the cushion protected almost nobody.

Consequence: bare --defaults output changed from the custom set to the library set, intentionally. Stored include_* answers drive rendering, so copier update on existing projects is unaffected apart from a one-time re-prompt of the preset question when its stored value is no longer a valid choice. The template-ci minimal scenario adds include_examples=false to stay a true core-only render.

docs.title: The example input file holds identity answers and a preset only
docs.text:
Id: ef5a9b93-2be9-4b18-a354-4a6c174207fe Type: decision Status: active Evidence: confirmed Source: ADR-016 (docs/adr/016-archetype-based-presets.md) Revisit when: the identity questions gain defaults, or non-interactive generation gets another data source

.example-input.yml carries only the no-default identity answers, the free-form keywords and preset: library; the per-toggle include_*: false lines were removed. The file is kept, not deleted.

Reason: removing the toggle list deletes the recurring maintenance step "update the example input when a toggle is added", so the file becomes stable. It stays because the identity fields have no defaults and giving them defaults would be a footgun — a bare --defaults run would emit a project literally named example owned by octocat — while non-interactive generation (the example task, the CI render job) still needs a data source. The render harness is unaffected; it supplies its own identity dictionary through Copier's API.

Rejected alternative: remove the file and give the identity questions defaults — the footgun above.

docs.title: release-please is the sole release orchestrator
docs.text:
Id: 7ec8a937-fd4d-41f2-96b7-824fe3be913b Type: decision Status: active Evidence: confirmed Source: ADR-002 (docs/adr/002-release-please-for-release-automation.md); validated against the keycast release pipeline (keycast#11) Revisit when: the open re-evaluation below is decided, or the generated project's version stops being sourced from git tags See: release-automation.md#the-release-automation-choice-is-under-re-evaluation — d9131d49-3c27-48f8-a903-e97caf4acff6 — as of 2026-10-11 See: package-distribution.md#optional-pypi-publishing — 20be7463-ca95-4d01-82c9-71f632d1b4be — as of 2026-10-12

Every generated project ships an unconditional release-please pipeline in one unified release.yml: Conventional Commits on main open a release PR, its merge cuts the tag and release, and every downstream job (build, PyPI — optional since ADR-039 —, executables, Docker, docs, SBOM, notifications) gates on its outputs. The former release_automation choice (none, release-please, release-it, release-drafter) and the separate cd.yml are gone. Versioning is sourced from git tags through hatch-vcs, so release-please never edits a version literal and uv.lock cannot desync; bump-minor-pre-major keeps pre-1.0 projects pre-1.0.

Reason: offering three tools multiplied the integration surface for a feature each project configures once. release-please is Python-native, derives the version from commits the template already enforces, and produces a reviewable release PR before any tag exists. Two of the three hard-won keycast fixes were already in the template, so it was the option with the most evidence.

Rejected alternative: release-it — JS-oriented, needs a Node runtime, and a human picks the bump every time.

Rejected alternative: release-drafter — label-driven, writes release notes but no CHANGELOG.md.

Rejected alternative: keeping a none escape hatch — projects that want no automation delete the files after generation; accepted for a template whose audience publishes releases.

Consequence: the PyPI trusted publisher must register release.yml as the workflow. Rendering plus actionlint validate the workflow across option combinations, but draft-tag timing, OIDC publishing and reconciliation can only be exercised by a live release. The template has no CHANGELOG.md seed file: release-please owns the changelog, and a scaffold-time seed would wipe an adopting project's release history on update.

docs.title: The release is created as a draft, finalized after artifacts attach
docs.text:
Id: 398b3cd9-e57b-4856-b2c7-76752c0ec37f Type: decision Status: active Evidence: confirmed Source: ADR-002 (docs/adr/002-release-please-for-release-automation.md); the wrong-version bug caught in cobo#49 Revisit when: release-please creates releases after artifact upload natively, or computes its commit range from drafts See: release-automation.md#release-please-is-the-sole-release-orchestrator — 7ec8a937-fd4d-41f2-96b7-824fe3be913b — as of 2026-10-11

release-please creates the GitHub release with draft: true and force-tag-creation: true. Build jobs attach wheels, executables and the SBOM to the draft; finalize-release un-drafts it and then closes the phantom next-release PR and re-dispatches the workflow, bounded.

Reason: a public release must never exist without its artifacts, so the release stays a draft until they are attached. GitHub withholds a draft's git tag until publication, so without forced tag creation the build job would run before the tag exists and hatch-vcs would stamp the previous version. The phantom PR exists because release-please computes its commit range from the latest published release and ignores drafts.

Rejected alternative: draft: false — a window with a public release and no artifacts.

Consequence: docs deployment lives in the same workflow (deploy-docs, after finalization) because an event fired by finalize-release's token cannot trigger a separate workflow.

docs.title: The workflow_dispatch trigger on release.yml stays; the publish environment is the containment
docs.text:
Id: 0d93a35d-46a3-4ac6-b072-fc07da789842 Type: decision Type: constraint Status: active Evidence: confirmed Source: ADR-002 (docs/adr/002-release-please-for-release-automation.md) Revisit when: the GitHub API for re-running a workflow stops requiring the dispatch trigger, or environment deployment-branch policies change See: release-automation.md#the-release-is-created-as-a-draft-finalized-after-artifacts-attach — 398b3cd9-e57b-4856-b2c7-76752c0ec37f — as of 2026-10-11 See: supply-chain-security.md#provenance-minting-shares-the-protected-publication-boundary — a0396603-cb34-4151-9d5b-1fc77eb31f6e — as of 2026-10-11

release.yml keeps workflow_dispatch. The publish jobs run in a publish environment whose deployment-branch policy is limited to main; the generated setup guide ships that policy as a scriptable step with a check, because GitHub auto-creates the environment unprotected on first use.

Reason: the trigger looks like a publish-escalation surface — a manual run executes the workflow file from the selected branch, so the release_created guard cannot stop someone with write access from dispatching a guard-free copy and minting a trusted-publishing token. But finalize-release's reconciliation re-dispatches the workflow through the API, which requires the trigger. GitHub evaluates an environment's branch policy outside the workflow file, so the environment contains what the trigger exposes.

Rejected alternative: remove the trigger — breaks release-PR reconciliation.

docs.title: Release workflows use GITHUB_TOKEN, with two documented manual workarounds
docs.text:
Id: bc96b93e-9b9e-4496-8fbb-b215f1d9a04c Type: decision Type: workaround Status: active Evidence: confirmed Source: ADR-002 (docs/adr/002-release-please-for-release-automation.md); issue #332 Revisit when: GitHub lets the workflow token start workflow runs or grants it workflow write access See: release-automation.md#release-please-is-the-sole-release-orchestrator — 7ec8a937-fd4d-41f2-96b7-824fe3be913b — as of 2026-10-11

Release-please runs with the implicit GITHUB_TOKEN. Two consequences are handled procedurally in the generated setup guide rather than with a stronger credential: the release PR reports no required status contexts until a human closes and reopens it, and a merge that changes workflow files between the release PR merging and the release run finishing must wait, because the release API then refuses tag creation with a 403.

Reason: events created with the workflow token do not start workflow runs, and the token cannot be granted workflow write access. A PAT or App token would fix both but is a standing credential with write access to main; closing and reopening the PR (every required context listens for reopened) and pausing workflow merges are the cheaper side of that trade. Editing the PR body is not equivalent — two of the checks do not listen for edited.

Rejected alternative: a PAT or GitHub App token for release-please.

docs.title: The stale draft-release comment link is an accepted cosmetic defect
docs.text:
Id: 2c6a6034-1936-4026-b10a-93445ace87b1 Type: decision Status: active Evidence: confirmed Source: ADR-002 (docs/adr/002-release-please-for-release-automation.md); issue #143, PR #152 Revisit when: release-please rewrites its release comment after un-drafting, or the draft flow is replaced See: release-automation.md#the-release-is-created-as-a-draft-finalized-after-artifacts-attach — 398b3cd9-e57b-4856-b2c7-76752c0ec37f — as of 2026-10-11

release-please posts its "created releases" comment once, at draft-creation time, with the transient untagged-<hash> slug; after finalization that link 404s. It is left as is.

Reason: the release, tag, artifacts and SBOM are all correct; only a link on an already-merged PR is dead. draft: false would repair the link but reintroduce the no-artifacts window, and having finalize-release patch the comment adds API surface for no functional gain.

Rejected alternative: patch the comment in finalize-release — still available without switching tools, listed as an option in the re-evaluation.

docs.title: Commitizen is a commit helper, never a release tool
docs.text:
Id: ee1d2fad-67ab-4f4a-a531-73458da14eb1 Type: decision Status: active Evidence: confirmed Source: ADR-004 (docs/adr/004-commitizen-as-commit-helper-not-release-tool.md) Revisit when: the re-evaluation below selects a Commitizen-based orchestrator See: release-automation.md#release-please-is-the-sole-release-orchestrator — 7ec8a937-fd4d-41f2-96b7-824fe3be913b — as of 2026-10-11

The generated [tool.commitizen] block contains only the convention name. The release-coupled keys (tag format, version provider and scheme, major_version_zero, changelog-on-bump) were removed, so cz bump has no configured tagging or changelog behaviour. The commit-message hooks stay; Commitizen is always included (the include_commitizen toggle was dropped because its hooks were unconditional anyway).

Reason: as shipped, Commitizen was configured as a second complete release pipeline that tags the same releases and rewrites the same CHANGELOG.md as release-please — a direct conflict the first release decision never compared. Versioning, tagging and changelog get exactly one owner; Commitizen keeps the orthogonal half, helping to write and lint conforming commits.

Rejected alternative: keep both configured as "aligned" — competing tags and two changelog writers on one file.

Consequence: message linting overlaps the PR-title check under the required squash-by-title merge strategy; accepted because the hook gives feedback while authoring, before a PR exists.

docs.title: The release-automation choice is under re-evaluation
docs.text:
Id: d9131d49-3c27-48f8-a903-e97caf4acff6 Type: decision Status: open Evidence: confirmed Source: ADR-037 (docs/adr/037-release-automation-reevaluation.md), a research record last refreshed 2026-10-05; upstream release-please issues #2515 and #2605 Revisit when: git-cliff ships prerelease version calculation (#1380), RC series become frequent, or a maintainer picks one of the four options See: release-automation.md#release-please-is-the-sole-release-orchestrator — 7ec8a937-fd4d-41f2-96b7-824fe3be913b — as of 2026-10-11 See: release-automation.md#commitizen-is-a-commit-helper-never-a-release-tool — ee1d2fad-67ab-4f4a-a531-73458da14eb1 — as of 2026-10-11

Two friction points reopened the tool choice: a stable release cut after release candidates lists only changes since the last RC (release-please has no prerelease/stable distinction and no config remedy; the npm CLI team works around the same behaviour by hand), and the draft-then-finalize dance plus phantom-PR reconciliation are workarounds layered on release-please's model. The research frames tools as commit helpers, changelog engines and release orchestrators, and compares Commitizen (cz bump, fixes the RC range with one setting, medium effort, reverses the commit-helper decision, loses the reviewable release PR) against git-cliff (a changelog engine only; high effort, RC math stays hand-written). Four options stand: stay and document, migrate to Commitizen, git-cliff inside a bespoke orchestrator, or defer. Until decided, nothing changes.

Why this needs an answer: both replacements need a standing privileged credential or a maintainer-local bump under the full preset's ruleset, and release.yml fans out to every generated project while being validated only by rendering until a live release runs. Whether the RC gap bites often enough to justify that blast radius is a maintainer judgement, not a research result.

docs.title: Optional Docker Hub configuration gates the publish fan-out
docs.text:
Id: f6f9eea4-dd38-4a74-98ed-f67e436c393d Type: decision Status: active Evidence: confirmed Source: PR #51, shared-gate review discussion; commit f48250e Verification: corroborated — the web release workflow makes both PyPI and Docker publication depend on docker-publish-preflight Revisit when: a new irreversible publication channel is added or Docker Hub opt-in semantics change

Docker Hub publication is optional and its credential pair is all-or-nothing: neither credential means GHCR-only publication, both enable Docker Hub, and a partial pair fails a shared preflight before either PyPI or Docker publication.

Reason: PyPI uploads are irreversible. A credential check inside only the Docker job would allow PyPI publication to finish concurrently before Docker failed, stranding a partially published release. The shared prerequisite rejects that known configuration error before the publish jobs fan out; it does not make all later external uploads transactional.

Rejected alternative: validate the credentials only inside Docker publication. Review moved the check into a shared prerequisite specifically to prevent the PyPI race. Requiring Docker Hub for every web release is not the selected contract; GHCR-only publication remains supported.

The narrowly scoped ghalint exceptions exist because conditional steps need job-scoped credential-presence information and GitHub does not expose the secrets context directly in conditions. The token itself is reduced to a presence flag, not exposed job-wide. The exceptions are recorded in the generated .github/ghalint.yaml rather than disabling that policy globally.

docs.title: Released-issue notifications are one inline job in release.yml
docs.text:
Id: c8cd015d-12ff-47a7-9447-40b69a2b1a82 Type: decision Status: active Evidence: confirmed Source: ADR-010 §2 (docs/adr/010-pr-docs-previews-and-released-issue-notifications.md) Revisit when: the release lifecycle is split across workflows See: release-automation.md#the-release-is-created-as-a-draft-finalized-after-artifacts-attach — 398b3cd9-e57b-4856-b2c7-76752c0ec37f — as of 2026-10-11

A notify-released-issues job, gated on a created release and running after finalization, uses a single inline github-script step to comment the release tag and URL on every issue the release closed. It is always on, with no toggle.

Reason: the upstream implementation shipped a committed Python script and a JS helper behind a reusable workflow — more moving parts than a single-maintainer project needs. Inline in release.yml matches keeping the whole release lifecycle in one workflow, and it is zero-config: no closed issues means no notification, so it cannot fail an unused feature.

Rejected alternative: a separate workflow_call file with committed scripts.

docs.title: Repository configuration as code and maintainer setup
Repository metadata via the Settings GitHub App, opt-in; labels and branch protection stay out of it
docs.text:
Id: dee6eadb-b617-4d64-bbec-7c688bad0604 Type: decision Status: active Evidence: confirmed Source: ADR-018 (docs/adr/018-repository-settings-as-code.md) Revisit when: GitHub exposes the About-sidebar activity toggles through an API, or the Settings App gains rulesets support See: external-integrations.md#a-freshly-generated-project-is-green-on-first-push-with-zero-external-accounts — 392b6dcf-6e9d-441d-bf7b-64ba362578d7 — as of 2026-10-11 See: repo-setup.md#branch-protection-as-code-through-an-opt-in-rulesets-sync-workflow — 3f94789f-94e8-4758-a32d-1e0d72c0140b — as of 2026-10-11

include_repo_settings (default off, full preset only) renders .github/settings.yml for the Settings App: description, homepage, topics (normalized from a free-form answer and omitted when empty so existing topics stay untouched) and the squash-merge flags release-please needs. Labels are excluded; branch protection and collaborators are excluded. The activity toggles cannot be set by anything.

Reason: the App is an external install, so opt-in. Labels are already managed App-free by an always-on label-sync workflow, and moving them under an opt-in App would drop the provisioning of the no-issue label that the linked-issue check needs as its bypass. Branch protection was excluded as duplicating the documented required-checks setup — a part later superseded by the rulesets workflow below. The activity toggles are web-UI only.

Rejected alternative: consolidate labels under the App — breaks the linked-issue escape hatch for any project without the App.

Consequence: the App escalates push access to admin, mitigated by the documented CODEOWNERS plus required code-owner review pattern.

docs.title: Branch protection as code through an opt-in Rulesets sync workflow
docs.text:
Id: 3f94789f-94e8-4758-a32d-1e0d72c0140b Type: decision Status: active Evidence: confirmed Source: ADR-021 (docs/adr/021-repository-ruleset-as-code.md) Revisit when: the workflow token can manage rulesets, the Settings App supports them, or a project needs required human approvals See: repo-setup.md#repository-metadata-via-the-settings-github-app-opt-in-labels-and-branch-protection-stay-out-of-it — dee6eadb-b617-4d64-bbec-7c688bad0604 — as of 2026-10-11

include_repo_ruleset (default off, full preset) scaffolds a canonical ruleset JSON for the default branch — no deletion or force push, linear history, pull requests with squash-only merges and thread resolution, zero required approvals, no bypass actors, strict required status checks naming the template's real contexts (the task-list gate as its check run Task Completed Checker, not its job name) — and an idempotent sync workflow authenticated by a REPO_ADMIN_TOKEN fine-grained PAT that warns and skips when the secret is absent.

Reason: a generated repository ships exactly the checks to gate merges on but none is enforced until an admin hand-wires protection — the per-project drift the template designs away. The Settings App cannot manage rulesets and the workflow token cannot be granted administration, so a PAT is required. Zero required approvals avoids deadlocking solo maintainers on their own PRs and unblocks release-please and Renovate while still enforcing every check. Requiring the task-list job name would gate nothing: the job is green with boxes unticked, so the check run it publishes is what must be required.

Rejected alternative: classic branch protection — a ruleset is one declarative, export-friendly file, which weakens the earlier duplication concern.

Consequence: strict status checks mean concurrent bot PRs rebase before merging; manual web-UI ruleset edits are reverted on the next push.

docs.title: Maintainer repository setup has one actor-tagged home in the docs tree
docs.text:
Id: 4e0fcdab-d3b9-4f96-b61d-8e34927af98d Type: decision Status: active Evidence: confirmed Source: ADR-022 (docs/adr/022-maintainer-setup-as-single-doc-home.md) Revisit when: the docs site is published before setup starts (making a published URL viable), or the setup guide moves See: docs-stack.md#the-sphinx-subsystem-is-toggleable-include_docs-default-on-the-maintainer-guide-is-not — e983d1e7-421f-4926-9415-a3da4626f220 — as of 2026-10-11

docs/maintaining/setup.rst is the single home for one-time owner setup, organized by concern with every step tagged [AGENT] (scriptable) or [HUMAN] (browser-only), published under a maintainer-guide toctree caption. CONTRIBUTING.md keeps the contributor-facing release narrative and a one-line pointer; README, the CI skip notices and the integration config files point at the .rst source path.

Reason: CONTRIBUTING.md had grown to ~590 lines, ~330 of them owner work a contributor never performs — a category error that also buried the contributor material. The guidance was scattered across six files pointing back at it. Actor tags are what make a setup skill tractable. The pointer is the repo-relative source path, not the published URL, because enabling the docs site is itself a setup step, so the URL 404s until setup is done. RST sections replaced a hand-maintained step counter that had to be bumped whenever a step was added, and RST keeps the guide under the existing docs lint and link-check gates.

Rejected alternative: a flat numbered list — the counter coupling above.

Rejected alternative: Markdown — outside the docs tooling that gates the other pages.

Consequence: the setup guide renders on the public docs site; it contains only the shape of the setup, no secrets.

docs.title: A resume-driven repo-setup skill reads [CHECK] blocks from the setup doc; no separate manifest
docs.text:
Id: 68ac4665-dcde-456b-aef7-2faaf6fe51f4 Type: decision Status: active Evidence: confirmed Source: ADR-023 (docs/adr/023-repo-setup-skill.md); the pattern follows the infra-setup skill in infra-copilot Revisit when: a setup step cannot carry a [CHECK] block, or the skill grows a parser instead of an LLM reader See: repo-setup.md#maintainer-repository-setup-has-one-actor-tagged-home-in-the-docs-tree — 4e0fcdab-d3b9-4f96-b61d-8e34927af98d — as of 2026-10-11 See: agent-instructions.md#ai-rulez-is-the-opt-in-single-source-for-agent-instructions-with-the-prose-in-shared-macros — e1545d12-ac20-426b-9cd5-519e80a56b5f — as of 2026-10-11 See: template-updates.md#copieryml-defines-no-_tasks — 86130379-1660-4992-8aba-8b6cd7b4a9f7 — as of 2026-10-11

Every actionable step in the setup doc carries a [CHECK] block: a command where exit 0 means the step is done. End-state checks assert the state a step establishes (not a weaker proxy); secret-presence checks assert the stored artifact by name, with conditional variants gated on repository attributes; steps with no API-visible artifact carry an explicit no-scriptable-check marker; steps covered by another step point at it. A skill shipped verbatim into every generated project walks the doc top to bottom without aborting, classifies steps as required, deferred (GitHub Pages and previews, expected red until the first release) or optional (asks configure-or-skip), and reports everything together. A symmetric repo-local skill drives this repository's own two-step setup inline, flagging its deliberate write-not-read workflow permission.

Reason: the prose was executed two lossy ways — a human hand-running commands, or an external plugin skill with its own hand-maintained verify list duplicating the doc. Neither knew per step whether it was already done, and setup is invisible to CI. A standalone steps.yaml manifest would re-encode the commands, actor tags and Jinja gating the doc already carries and drift against it — exactly what the single-home decision collapsed. The consumer is an LLM reader, not a parser, so RST readability suffices. Deferred classification is the fix for a naive walk deadlocking at Pages before reaching the rest. The skill is a rendered file, so it never needs a post-copy task.

Rejected alternative: a steps.yaml manifest — the drift above.

Consequence: every future setup step must carry a [CHECK] block to stay machine-drivable, as every step already had to carry an actor tag.

docs.title: An unavailable home directory permits placeholders, not shared-temp logging
docs.text:
Id: 1488d613-3cce-4249-ade8-3a6dacbaceec Type: decision Type: constraint Status: active Evidence: confirmed Source: PR #126, rejection of the temporary-log fallback; commit f47e6fc Verification: corroborated — core/dirs.py.jinja distinguishes home resolution from placeholder paths, and core/logging_setup.py.jinja disables file logging when home resolution fails Revisit when: logging initialization becomes lazy or the template adopts a verified user-private fallback directory

Logging attaches the console handler before attempting file logging. Failure to resolve the home directory disables file logging entirely; file-system errors with a resolved home also degrade to console-only logging. Directory values may still use a temporary-directory-derived Path as a placeholder, but the template does not automatically write logs there.

Reason: logger initialization can happen at module import, so unavailable or unwritable home storage must not crash read-only commands. A predictable shared temporary log path can be pre-created or symlinked by another local user; its existence as a valid Path does not establish safe ownership for writes.

Rejected alternative: automatically log under a shared temporary project directory when home resolution fails. The initial fallback was explicitly rejected because it creates a local log-hijacking opportunity.

Lazy file-handler initialization was suggested, but the reviewed evidence does not establish why it was not selected. The current cached logger accessor also does not make module-level calls lazy: caching prevents repeated setup, not the first import-time initialization.

docs.title: Three architecture-named executable toggles instead of one brand toggle
docs.text:
Id: d5aed1a0-0b7c-4ac3-9d75-fb9568d9e34d Type: decision Status: active Evidence: confirmed Source: ADR-007 (docs/adr/007-standalone-executable-toggles.md) Revisit when: a fourth standalone-executable architecture appears, or a category's strongest tool changes

include_launcher (PyCrucible, uv-bootstrap launcher), include_compiler (Nuitka, source-to-machine-code) and include_freezer (PyInstaller, interpreter-plus-deps bundle) replace the single include_pycrucible toggle. All three default to false and combine freely; there is no when: gating and no mutually exclusive choice.

Reason: the single toggle conflated a brand with a capability and covered one of three architectures that make materially different promises — a tiny online-first-run launcher, a compiled native binary, a fully offline bundle — and that a project may legitimately want together (a launcher for connected users and an offline bundle for air-gapped ones). Naming the architecture rather than the tool means swapping PyCrucible for PyApp later needs no variable rename.

Rejected alternative: one executable_tool enum — forces mutual exclusion that is wrong for these categories and blocks adding a fourth later.

Rejected alternative: PyApp or UVBox — same launcher category as PyCrucible, lateral not new capability. cx_Freeze and py2exe — weaker freezers (py2exe Windows-only). mypyc — module-level, not whole-app. Briefcase — targets native installers and GUI/mobile packaging, out of scope for a single-file executable. PyOxidizer — archived.

Consequence: a breaking rename for existing answers files with no automatic migration (Copier does not rename variables). Build dependencies live in the uv tool group and are Renovate-tracked like every other pin. Each toggle must be exercised independently and in combination.

docs.title: Executables are named per tool and OS and all target the package main module
docs.text:
Id: 1b37b4df-147f-4d71-8249-4003ecfe4302 Type: decision Status: active Evidence: confirmed Source: ADR-007 (docs/adr/007-standalone-executable-toggles.md) Revisit when: attach-github-release stops flattening downloaded artifacts by filename, or component selection moves out of __main__.py

Each build names its binary <pkg>-<tool>-<os-label> rather than a bare <pkg>. All three builds target the package's __main__.py, which was generalized from a CLI-only form into the single entry that selects and launches whichever component is enabled; with an executable toggle on but no runnable component selected, main() raises a SystemExit with an explanatory message.

Reason: the release job collects every executable artifact with merge-multiple, which flattens by filename — bare names made per-OS (and, with more than one toggle, per-tool) binaries silently overwrite each other and drop platforms from the release. One entrypoint keeps the PyInstaller spec, the Nuitka command and the PyCrucible config free of duplicated component conditionals and guarantees the binary runs the app rather than importing a module that never invokes it. A binary that builds and exits non-zero with a reason beats one that silently does nothing and looks broken.

Consequence: PyCrucible takes the name via its output option, Nuitka via --output-filename (otherwise a generic __main__.bin), PyInstaller is renamed after the build because its spec cannot see the CI matrix. The PyInstaller spec is rendered for reproducible builds and un-ignored in the generated .gitignore (the default *.spec ignore would keep it uncommitted and break the fresh-checkout release build); Nuitka's flags live in the mise task and CI step since it has no spec equivalent. The mise package task was split per architecture, which also fixed a latent bug where the whole mise.toml body sat in one raw block and rendered the PyCrucible task regardless of the toggle.

docs.title: Every executable toggle adds a PR-time build-check job
docs.text:
Id: 69443ac8-be5b-401a-b45d-53d19c54045c Type: decision Status: active Evidence: confirmed Source: ADR-007 (docs/adr/007-standalone-executable-toggles.md) Revisit when: the test suite starts exercising the built binary, or the per-OS build cost outweighs the signal

Each enabled toggle renders a per-OS, fail-fast: false build-<tool>-check job in ci.yml that builds the executable on every push and pull request, verifies the binary was produced, smoke-runs it with --help for a CLI project, uploads a short-retention preview artifact and gates the check job. It mirrors the release build commands but never publishes.

Reason: the test suite always runs the source tree, never the built binary, so a dependency or Python bump that breaks packaging would otherwise fail silently at release time instead of against the offending diff.

Rejected alternative: build only at release time — the previous state.

docs.title: Provenance minting shares the protected publication boundary
docs.text:
Id: a0396603-cb34-4151-9d5b-1fc77eb31f6e Type: decision Type: constraint Status: active Evidence: confirmed Source: issue #185, PR #318, review discussions on private availability and the trust boundary; commit cc7ce42 Verification: corroborated — the release build uses the publish environment, includes gated attestation steps and per-platform bundles, and installation docs constrain signer workflow and ref Revisit when: attestation availability, signer verification, or the publishing environment's branch policy changes

The release build attests the distributions it produces and retains the provenance bundles alongside the release artifacts. Matrix builds attest their own outputs. Attestation minting runs behind the same externally protected publish environment as package publication, with a main-only deployment policy configured during repository setup. Referencing the environment in workflow source alone does not prove that an adopter configured its live policy. Consumer verification identifies the release workflow and the main ref, not only the repository. The workflow enables attestation for public repositories and requires explicit opt-in for private ones.

Reason: repository identity alone does not prove that the intended protected release workflow built an artifact. A branch-dispatched workflow could otherwise mint repository-backed attestations for arbitrary outputs. GitHub evaluates the environment's deployment policy outside the dispatched workflow file, so that boundary also protects provenance minting. The private opt-in avoids breaking releases on plans without the necessary attestation support.

Rejected alternative: leave minting in an unprotected build job and verify only repository identity. Review rejected this weaker trust boundary.

Rejected alternative: attempt attestations unconditionally on private repositories. Review required explicit opt-in to preserve unsupported private release paths.

ADR-002 records why manual release dispatch remains necessary and why the environment must have a main-only policy. The verification procedure is in generated docs/installation.rst; this entry records why its signer constraints and the minting boundary exist.

docs.title: Relationship between GitHub provenance and PyPI attestations
docs.text:
Id: 09b24722-bfa5-460a-bbd7-05d8973b5389 Type: decision Status: superseded Evidence: unknown Source: issue #185, PyPI-side integration question; PR #318 Verification: uncorroborated — the reviewed sources establish the explicit GitHub provenance path, but no resolution of the PyPI-side overlap question was found See: supply-chain-security.md#provenance-minting-shares-the-protected-publication-boundary — a0396603-cb34-4151-9d5b-1fc77eb31f6e — as of 2026-10-08 Superseded by: f5495121-8004-4652-b3ac-af71995c263a

The proposal asked whether the trusted-publishing action's PEP 740 attestations make the explicit GitHub provenance step partly redundant, or whether both paths serve a deliberate belt-and-suspenders purpose. The implementation retains the GitHub path, but the rationale for its relationship to PyPI-side attestations could not be recovered. No historical reason for keeping both was established; this was not a finding that either mechanism was defective or safe to remove.

The current decision below resolves the configuration choice from verified technical differences. It does not turn that new justification into a claim about the original implementation's intent.

docs.title: Retain build provenance and publication attestations as distinct claims
docs.text:
Id: f5495121-8004-4652-b3ac-af71995c263a Type: decision Status: active Evidence: confirmed Source: current attestation review, 2026-10-08; PyPI Publish predicate, PyPI attestation production, GitHub artifact attestations; pinned PyPI action dc37677, action.yml defaults and attestations.py signing implementation Verification: corroborated — the build job emits SLSA provenance, the separate PyPI job uses default Trusted Publishing attestations, and both consume the same distribution artifacts without rebuilding Revisit when: the publishing action changes its default predicate or the workflow changes artifact transfer or attestation storage See: supply-chain-security.md#provenance-minting-shares-the-protected-publication-boundary — a0396603-cb34-4151-9d5b-1fc77eb31f6e — as of 2026-10-08

The current configuration retains both mechanisms. GitHub's build step produces SLSA provenance at build time, with workflow/source/run information and artifact digests. The pinned PyPI action defaults to a PyPI Publish attestation during Trusted Publishing to PyPI or TestPyPI: its predicate body is empty, and its certificate identity identifies the publisher. It is not a second structured SLSA build statement. PEP 740 defines index-hosted attestation handling rather than requiring that all attestations make the same claim.

Reason: the claims and consumer channels complement one another. GitHub stores build attestations and the template attaches their bundles to releases; PyPI exposes publication attestations through its per-file provenance APIs and UI. The publishing and release-attachment jobs download the built distributions without rebuilding them, preserving the artifact hashes. PyPI's default signing does not export the separately created GitHub build-provenance bundle to PyPI.

Rejected alternative: remove the explicit GitHub step because PyPI already signs attestations. The default publication claim does not replace the structured build claim or the build bundle distributed with GitHub Releases.

Rejected alternative: disable PyPI's default attestations as duplicate work. That would remove the index-hosted publication claim and its discovery channel. There is overlapping identity/integrity coverage, but neither path currently replaces all of the other's claims and availability.

GitHub's private-repository entitlement and explicit opt-in govern its build attestations only. The PyPI action has no equivalent repository-visibility gate; its default path requires Trusted Publishing and uses public Sigstore signing infrastructure. API-token publication or an explicit attestation opt-out changes that path. Main-only publication depends on the configured GitHub environment policy, not inferred merely from a PyPI publisher's repository/workflow registration.

The verification procedures and availability distinction are in generated docs/installation.rst. This is a present decision grounded in the documented mechanisms; the original rationale remains unknown in the superseded record.

docs.title: Unknown scan visibility fails open; private audits remain useful
docs.text:
Id: 8973c4ce-8e76-42fa-b69b-e52fc34eba50 Type: decision Type: workaround Status: active Evidence: confirmed Source: issue #293, PR #294, PR #291; commits 0e7fac8 and f19133d Verification: corroborated — CodeQL and Scorecard coalesce visibility sources with a public default; zizmor selects public SARIF or private inline annotations Revisit when: GitHub documents a reliable visibility source for scheduled runs or private scanning availability changes

CodeQL and Scorecard use two potential visibility sources and default an unknown result to public. Zizmor instead switches its output mode: public repositories use the code-scanning dashboard, while private/internal repositories keep the audit through inline annotations rather than a potentially unsupported upload.

Reason: scheduled runs lack the usual repository event payload, and the other visibility property was undocumented and runtime-unverified in the investigation. Silently skipping public security scans when both sources are empty is a worse failure than an unsupported private run reporting an error. Zizmor's push/PR events have the payload needed for its narrower mode selection; an unavailable private dashboard does not make the underlying audit useless.

Rejected alternative: guard scheduled scans with a single visibility source. It could silently disable analysis when that source is absent.

Rejected alternative: skip the entire private zizmor job. That discards an audit that can still report through annotations without code-scanning support.

The fallback rationale is confirmed by the sources; actual runtime availability of the undocumented visibility property remains unknown. Source inspection corroborates the implemented policy, not that property's runtime behavior. ADR-013 separately records MegaLinter's best-effort SARIF upload posture.

docs.title: Local and historical secret scanning cover different failure stages
docs.text:
Id: 62d903d7-45bb-4790-b28a-f5dd1934983a Type: decision Status: active Evidence: confirmed Source: issue #175, PR #236; commit 825f420; docs/template-architecture.md, secret scanning Verification: corroborated — generated prek config includes detect-secrets and a baseline, while the security workflow retains gitleaks history scanning Revisit when: either scanner's execution stage or baseline-management contract changes

Generated projects retain both a local, baseline-backed detect-secrets hook and history-spanning gitleaks in CI.

Reason: historical scanning detects exposure after a secret reaches commit history. A local hook can stop that commit before the exposure occurs. The committed baseline makes known false positives reviewable instead of requiring blanket scanner suppression. Similar-looking scanners are therefore deliberate layers, not redundant lint execution.

Rejected alternative: rely on historical gitleaks coverage alone. The issue identifies the missing before-commit gate as the reason for adding local scanning. Alternatives among other local scanning tools, and why they lost to detect-secrets, are unknown in the reviewed evidence.

The baseline maintenance procedure is in generated .github/CONTRIBUTING.md. ADR-003 covers the general fast-hook versus full-suite boundary; this entry records the distinct exposure stages.

docs.title: Render-and-inspect is the fast matrixed layer; generate-and-run stays separate
docs.text:
Id: c9bcdf52-af5d-4438-9c9f-d55e8226812c Type: decision Status: active Evidence: confirmed Source: ADR-024 (docs/adr/024-render-and-inspect-template-test-suite.md); issue #365 for the parallel run Revisit when: the golden set grows past a couple of stable artifacts, or a root Python project appears See: template-testing.md#toolsrenderpy-is-the-only-place-the-template-is-rendered — f41fa3a2-20e2-4ba5-a3d0-c53a0074a9d0 — as of 2026-10-11

tests/ renders the template through Copier's Python API into temp directories and asserts on the output tree: every preset renders, plus one render per broker and per web framework; every generated YAML parses; the rendered pyproject.toml is valid TOML; and pytest-regressions golden files snapshot pyproject.toml for the library and full presets only. It runs in template-ci.yml's render-tests job from an ephemeral uv env, in parallel.

Reason: the template's correctness across presets and toggle combinations had no automated guard — example/ covered one option set when a human remembered. A Jinja mistake emitting malformed YAML in a conditional file, or a whitespace regression in a guarded block, merged green. Rendering without installing is fast enough to fan out; pyproject.toml carries pins that move on every update, so a broad golden set would be churn without coverage.

Rejected alternative: pytest-copie — a terser fixture that does not earn a second dependency beyond copier.

Rejected alternative: only generate-and-run — proves the project works but is slow and heavy; "renders and is structurally valid" is a strictly weaker, far cheaper property, so the two layers stay separate.

Consequence: an intentional change to the two golden artifacts needs a regeneration and a reviewed diff.

docs.title: Generated files must be formatter-canonical, not merely valid
docs.text:
Id: 9b931598-7e52-4ff1-bb07-ef65c01d5369 Type: decision Type: constraint Type: incident Status: active Evidence: confirmed Source: ADR-030 (docs/adr/030-generated-files-must-be-formatter-canonical.md); issue #213 Revisit when: yamlfmt or taplo change the semantics of the pinned non-default knobs, or the generated project's formatter set changes See: template-testing.md#render-and-inspect-is-the-fast-matrixed-layer-generate-and-run-stays-separate — c9bcdf52-af5d-4438-9c9f-d55e8226812c — as of 2026-10-11

A generated file must already be in the exact byte form the generated project's own formatters produce — yamlfmt, ruff-format, the prek builtins and taplo. Three things follow: formatter config is chosen so the hand-written layout is canonical (retain_line_breaks_single for yamlfmt; no array auto-expand, auto-collapse or comment alignment for taplo; no yamlfmt max_line_length); template sources are written in that form (one-line folded scalars, no comment trailing a sequence, TOML arrays one-per-line with trailing comma, Jinja whitespace control so no conditional leaves more than two blank lines or one at EOF, literal UTF-8 author tokens instead of tojson); and taplo runs in strict check mode. template-ci.yml's render job runs the rendered project's own fixing hooks per scenario and gates on git diff, with an integrations scenario and a non-ASCII author name covering toggles nothing else rendered.

Reason: on a pristine scaffold the first hook run rewrote two workflow files and taplo rewrote two TOML files while exiting 0, so the adopter's hooks CI failed and every later copier update showed drift they never caused. Nothing caught it because this repo ran only checking tools over a render and the harness asserts YAML parses, not that it is canonical; taplo's fix mode made the defect invisible. Width-driven reflow would make a file's canonical form depend on which components are enabled, and comment alignment would let a Renovate bump break a line nothing touched. The diff, not hook exit codes, is the gate because a fixing hook that rewrites and exits 0 sails through an exit-code check.

Rejected alternative: chase the formatters' output in the templates — the config is pinned to make the written layout canonical instead.

Consequence: hand-aligned trailing comments and hand-wrapped folded scalars are unavailable; a conditional block in rendered YAML/TOML requires thinking about whitespace control; the pinned knobs fail loudly if a release changes them.

docs.title: Collection literals are rendered through one shared macro
docs.text:
Id: 47b21a49-5fc4-46b8-b450-7d9f3225706c Type: decision Status: active Evidence: confirmed Source: ADR-030, 2026-09 amendment (docs/adr/030-generated-files-must-be-formatter-canonical.md); the agent-prose macros in the same file are recorded in ADR-035 Revisit when: ruff-format changes its magic-trailing-comma or width behaviour, or Copier gains a way to share helpers inside _subdirectory See: template-testing.md#generated-files-must-be-formatter-canonical-not-merely-valid — 9b931598-7e52-4ff1-bb07-ef65c01d5369 — as of 2026-10-11

py_collection(name, items, kind) in _macros.jinja emits a tuple or list literal in the form ruff-format produces: one line when the statement fits in 88 columns, one element per line otherwise. The file sits at the repository root, outside _subdirectory, and templates import it on their first line. It is used for __all__, the dependency allowlists and the guard tuples.

Reason: a literal rendered from a Jinja loop has no single correct spelling — the width depends on values known only at render time (package name, broker module, component count) — so a template that always emits one form ships a file the adopter's first hook run rewrites. Outside _subdirectory the file is an input Copier can never render into a project and needs no _exclude override, which would replace Copier's default exclude list wholesale.

Rejected alternative: a second hand-written copy of the width branch — the drift this replaced.

docs.title: tools/render.py is the only place the template is rendered
docs.text:
Id: f41fa3a2-20e2-4ba5-a3d0-c53a0074a9d0 Type: decision Type: constraint Status: active Evidence: confirmed Source: ADR-031 §1 (docs/adr/031-single-render-entrypoint.md); issues #181, #183, #164, #184 Revisit when: Copier's API changes, or a root pyproject.toml appears (it must keep the repo root importable under pytest) See: template-testing.md#render-and-inspect-is-the-fast-matrixed-layer-generate-and-run-stays-separate — c9bcdf52-af5d-4438-9c9f-d55e8226812c — as of 2026-10-11

A plain Python module with PEP 723 metadata wraps copier.run_copy. The render harness fixture, the generate-and-run CI matrix, the committed docs artifacts, the watch loop and the mise tasks all call it. Answers layer as a neutral identity, then --data-file, then explicit answers; programmatic renders use only the neutral identity so golden files stay stable regardless of a maintainer's own example input. The CI matrix's kitchen-sink scenario is spelled as the full preset rather than a hand-listed toggle set.

Reason: "render this template with these answers" had forked into the harness, an inline CI invocation, the example task and three proposals each adding a script — six spellings where the answers baseline, the vcs_ref or the defaults handling can quietly disagree, and a CI matrix rendering a shape no other consumer can reproduce. A Python module, not a shell script, because the pytest harness must import the same code path. The preset spelling means a component added to full is exercised end-to-end without editing the matrix.

Rejected alternative: per-purpose shell scripts — two renderers again.

Consequence: adding another copier copy invocation is a review defect; a new consumer imports render() or calls the CLI.

docs.title: The generated-project tree page is a committed derived artifact with two drift guards
docs.text:
Id: 54918c4d-49dd-4ce8-94a6-3d472010173f Type: decision Status: active Evidence: confirmed Source: ADR-031 §2–3 (docs/adr/031-single-render-entrypoint.md); generalizes the cobo drift-guard posture of ADR-012 Revisit when: copier is pinned in the render path, or another derived artifact joins regenerate See: template-testing.md#toolsrenderpy-is-the-only-place-the-template-is-rendered — f41fa3a2-20e2-4ba5-a3d0-c53a0074a9d0 — as of 2026-10-11 See: ci-topology.md#network-dependent-checks-run-on-a-weekly-cron-never-in-the-merge-gate — 3e5b9525-9087-4125-b19f-80f6c226c01f — as of 2026-10-11 See: gitignore-generation.md#cobo-generates-the-gitignore-with-a-hash-sealed-fence-and-lockfiles — 3e3bc38e-bc1e-4e65-b74d-e91848262157 — as of 2026-10-11

regenerate renders the four presets and writes the exact file set each produces into docs/generated-project-trees.md, committed, plain fenced blocks. Two guards, one per direction of drift: a blocking test in render-tests asserts the committed page equals a fresh render (this repo changed), and a weekly non-blocking artifact-drift.yml regenerates and diffs (the toolchain changed underneath, since copier is installed unpinned). Golden files are not folded into regenerate.

Reason: the documented structure of a generated project is the first thing a scaffolding template's docs get wrong, and a hand-maintained page cannot show "this toggle adds these five files" as review signal. Committed rather than built into a gitignored directory precisely for that diff; example/ stays gitignored because a diff-based guard cannot apply to an untracked tree. A PR-time check cannot see a new copier release changing the output with no commit here. Golden files already have the same job and their own regeneration path.

Consequence: a PR changing what a preset renders must regenerate the page or fail render-tests; regenerate is the extension point for future derived artifacts.

docs.title: The watch loop is an authoring aid whose target is validated before every rebake
docs.text:
Id: 36ddff82-32d4-4234-a9cf-ea40d694df58 Type: decision Status: active Evidence: confirmed Source: ADR-031 §5 (docs/adr/031-single-render-entrypoint.md) Revisit when: the rebake stops removing its target tree See: template-testing.md#toolsrenderpy-is-the-only-place-the-template-is-rendered — f41fa3a2-20e2-4ba5-a3d0-c53a0074a9d0 — as of 2026-10-11

watch re-renders into a gitignored directory on every save under the template sources and survives a failed render. Its output path is rejected when it touches a watched source in either direction, or when it is a non-empty directory without a .copier-answers.yml. watchfiles is supplied by the mise task, not declared by the script.

Reason: each rebake removes its target tree. "Do not delete what this tool did not render" is checkable; enumerating which directories are precious is not. No other consumer should pay for a dependency only the loop needs.

docs.title: Renovate's copier manager delivers downstream updates; the template keeps release-please as its tag source
docs.text:
Id: f26da4b3-8b97-4cfc-9aba-64eba4acf04f Type: decision Status: active Evidence: confirmed Source: ADR-015 (docs/adr/015-template-self-versioning-and-copier-update-automation.md); prompted by hwid#113 Revisit when: Renovate fails its artifacts check on conflict markers (renovate#31600), or the copier manager accepts Copier's gh: shorthand See: release-automation.md#release-please-is-the-sole-release-orchestrator — 7ec8a937-fd4d-41f2-96b7-824fe3be913b — as of 2026-10-11 See: template-updates.md#copieryml-defines-no-_tasks — 86130379-1660-4992-8aba-8b6cd7b4a9f7 — as of 2026-10-11

Generated projects receive template updates through Renovate's first-party copier manager, which watches the template's git tags, runs the real copier update and opens a PR. No bespoke workflow ships. This repository's own release-please therefore must keep cutting tags — they are the datasource. Scaffolding uses the .git HTTPS URL because the gh: shorthand is not a git URL and the git-tags datasource rejects it silently.

Reason: nothing in a generated project watched for template changes and the template published no tags, so a default copier update found nothing. The template already ships Renovate as the canonical updater; its App token can push workflow files (the repo GITHUB_TOKEN cannot), and its PRs flow through the existing dashboard and review. Tags are cheap since release-please already runs and give adopters a changelog besides.

Rejected alternative: a bespoke copier-update.yml workflow — ~50 lines of security-sensitive YAML per project, and its default token cannot push .github/workflows/*, forcing every consumer to provision a PAT.

Rejected alternative: fohte/copier-update-action — the bespoke workflow as a third-party action, same token and conflict characteristics, plus an external action to trust with --trust.

Rejected alternative: drop the template's own versioning and track HEAD — the copier manager is tag-based, so release-please is the price of Renovate.

Consequence: a copier-update PR can look mergeable while carrying conflict markers; maintainers review for them. A repo pinned to a raw SHA needs one manual update to re-anchor onto a tag.

docs.title: copier.yml defines no _tasks
docs.text:
Id: 86130379-1660-4992-8aba-8b6cd7b4a9f7 Type: decision Type: constraint Status: active Evidence: confirmed Source: ADR-015 (docs/adr/015-template-self-versioning-and-copier-update-automation.md); the constraint is re-affirmed in ADR-018, ADR-023, ADR-024 and ADR-035 Revisit when: the hosted Renovate App allows --trust, or Copier marks tasks safe See: template-updates.md#renovates-copier-manager-delivers-downstream-updates-the-template-keeps-release-please-as-its-tag-source — f26da4b3-8b97-4cfc-9aba-64eba4acf04f — as of 2026-10-11

The template has no post-copy tasks; the former git init task is gone and the scaffold instructions tell the adopter to run it. Every later feature that needs a post-render step (the repo-setup skill, the render harness, the ai-rulez generator) is a rendered file or a documented command, never a task.

Reason: any task marks a template unsafe and forces --trust, which Renovate gates behind a self-hosted-only setting the hosted App disables — a task-bearing template makes the hosted App's copier update fail.

Rejected alternative: keep the git init task — breaks the update path for every hosted-Renovate adopter.

docs.title: Shipped template/** pins are frozen from this repository's Renovate
docs.text:
Id: 86e0af71-9614-42c1-9363-d16170d942a8 Type: decision Type: constraint Status: active Evidence: confirmed Source: ADR-020 (docs/adr/020-freeze-shipped-template-pins-from-renovate.md); the confirmed conflict source was PR #196 Revisit when: seed staleness becomes a security concern faster than downstream Renovate catches up, or Renovate learns to skip lines the downstream already moved See: template-updates.md#renovates-copier-manager-delivers-downstream-updates-the-template-keeps-release-please-as-its-tag-source — f26da4b3-8b97-4cfc-9aba-64eba4acf04f — as of 2026-10-11

A packageRules entry in .github/renovate.json matches template/** and disables updates there. Shipped version literals (action SHAs, prek rev pins, mise tool versions, dependency pins) are seed values only; each generated project's own Renovate owns them afterwards. This repository's root workflows, prek.toml and mise.toml stay Renovate-managed.

Reason: copier update is a 3-way merge per file, and a pinned line conflicts when both sides moved it to different values. Both repositories' bots advanced the same literals on independent schedules, so copier-update PRs conflicted on nearly every release — and Renovate does not fail on those conflicts, so a PR looked mergeable with markers inside. With the template frozen, "theirs" equals "base" on every pin line and the downstream's value wins cleanly: the conflict class is eliminated structurally. matchFileNames plus enabled: false rather than ignorePaths preserves the shared preset's own ignore list and composes with its digest-pinning policy.

Rejected alternative: auto-resolve in the downstream's favour via a merge=ours driver or copier _exclude — _exclude is whole-file and would block genuine template changes; a per-downstream merge driver is fragile.

Rejected alternative: converge by cadence (group bumps, release immediately) — only shrinks the race window.

Consequence: new projects start with slightly stale but valid seeds and their own Renovate opens catch-up PRs; refreshing seeds before a release is a deliberate act that reintroduces conflicts for projects not yet caught up. Re-enabling Renovate for template/** reads as fixing staleness but rebuilds the conflict engine.

docs.title: Retired template modules become adopter-owned
docs.text:
Id: 4dd6729a-697e-4588-a7a7-d37152018b6b Type: decision Type: constraint Status: active Evidence: confirmed Source: PR #333, version-sweep results; commits c150ec3 and 0f7a406 Verification: corroborated — copier.yml excludes the retired paths and requires Copier 9.10.3; the update skill records the same compatibility floor Revisit when: Copier changes update-deletion semantics or a retired module is rendered again See: components.md#one-application-payload-in-coreapppy-components-are-adapters-over-it — 8bb1e55e-f468-44fc-80a5-d3b3719e5ddc — as of 2026-10-11

The dropped utils/app.py and library-only core/app.py placeholders are excluded from updates, leaving existing copies under the adopter's ownership. The custom exclusion list explicitly retains Copier's default exclusions because _exclude replaces that list rather than extending it.

Reason: an adopter can have replaced a placeholder with real application code. Removing the template file can delete that edited copy without conflict markers or reject files, so ordinary conflict review cannot catch the loss. The recorded version sweep found that Copier 9.6.0–9.10.2 still deleted the excluded files; 9.10.3 and later preserved them. The version floor makes an older Copier refuse the update instead of silently deleting adopter code.

Rejected alternative: let normal template deletion remove the old modules. Rejected because the files may no longer be empty placeholders in the adopter.

Rejected alternative: use exclusions without raising the Copier minimum. Rejected because the version sweep showed the protection was ineffective on older supported versions.

The architectural reason for retiring the placeholders is the shared application payload entry in components.md; this entry records the distinct ownership and update-safety constraint.

docs.title: Adoption audits preserve behavior before consolidating workflows
docs.text:
Id: dfd6cd98-9d07-4dc4-b58f-d1343d636ea4 Type: decision Status: active Evidence: confirmed Source: issue #348, PR #349; commit 0abcffc; docs/template-adoption.md Verification: corroborated — the shipped template-adoption skill and its walkthrough compare behavior and preserve customizations; the older update skill now shares that contract Revisit when: the adoption and update skills change their reconciliation contract See: repo-setup.md#a-resume-driven-repo-setup-skill-reads-check-blocks-from-the-setup-doc-no-separate-manifest — 68ac4665-dcde-456b-aef7-2faaf6fe51f4 — as of 2026-10-11

The shipped adoption skill treats template defaults as evidence to compare with existing project behavior, rather than automatic authority to replace it. It handles initial adoption, updates, and audits of already-committed updates; repository-settings changes remain the responsibility of repo-setup.

Reason: two workflows that both run prek can differ in event coverage and required-check identity. Consolidating them can discard manual dispatch or leave live branch protection waiting for a check that no longer exists. A local ruleset file alone cannot establish the live requirements. A post-update audit can compare the actual committed baseline and diff without rerunning Copier and disturbing the state being inspected.

Alternatives considered: retain both workflows, accepting duplicate PR execution, or consolidate after preserving event coverage and transitioning the required check. The documented walkthrough deliberately makes that choice conditional on the adopter's decision and evidence; neither option is rejected universally. Deletion without establishing equivalence is excluded because it can silently remove functionality or block merges.

The execution procedure is in docs/template-adoption.md.

docs.title: Which reconciliation policy governs machine-config and CI conflicts?
docs.text:
Id: 3f155d92-8518-4294-bfcd-26251c36e2e1 Type: constraint Status: superseded Evidence: unknown Source: skills/update/SKILL.md, Shared reconciliation; the shipped template-adoption skill; PR #349 Verification: uncorroborated — the original justification for category-based precedence could not be established; the conflicting wording found during recovery has since been replaced See: template-updates.md#adoption-audits-preserve-behavior-before-consolidating-workflows — dfd6cd98-9d07-4dc4-b58f-d1343d636ea4 — as of 2026-10-08 Superseded by: 9a6bf00c-33c1-4f0c-962e-7e960f9d2d58

At recovery, the two skills coexisted with conflicting guidance: the older update skill selected template-side CI/config hunks by category, while the newer adoption skill required behavioral preservation and decisions before consequential cleanup. The reviewed historical sources did not establish which policy governed their overlap or justify the older precedence rule.

The question has been resolved by the current decision below, rather than by claiming to have recovered the original justification.

docs.title: Update and adoption skills share preservation-first reconciliation
docs.text:
Id: 9a6bf00c-33c1-4f0c-962e-7e960f9d2d58 Type: decision Status: active Evidence: confirmed Source: maintainer-approved reconciliation-policy review, 2026-10-08; docs/template-adoption.md; skills/update/SKILL.md Verification: corroborated — the older update skill now preserves custom behavior, requires evidence for equivalence, and delegates repository-settings transitions to repo-setup Revisit when: either skill changes its scope or introduces a conflicting reconciliation policy See: template-updates.md#adoption-audits-preserve-behavior-before-consolidating-workflows — dfd6cd98-9d07-4dc4-b58f-d1343d636ea4 — as of 2026-10-08

Both skills use the same preservation-first contract. The older update skill runs or reconciles updates; the generated adoption skill additionally handles initial adoption and audits of completed updates. Those workflow differences do not justify opposite advice about the same project customization.

Reason: file category does not establish behavioral equivalence. CI and machine configuration can encode adopter-specific event coverage, permissions, required-check identity, hooks, and dependencies. Replacing a hunk on the basis of its category can discard functioning customizations despite a green lint run. Routine maintenance can proceed directly when equivalence is established within the requested update; consequential behavior changes need an explicit decision.

The contract applies to clean merges as well as conflicts. Recovery uses the actual pre-update snapshot and preserves later edits: a current base branch can lack branch-owned release history, while the index may already hold the reset.

Rejected alternative: retain automatic template precedence for CI/config hunks. It gives template origin more authority than evidence of the adopter's existing behavior. Even action digest updates require checking release effects and preserving configured inputs rather than assuming equivalence from the SHA.

Repository-settings transitions remain with repo-setup; the reconciliation procedure is in the skills, not duplicated here. The former policy's historical justification remains unknown in the superseded record above.

docs.title: Copier over Cookiecutter, Cruft, Yeoman and GitHub template repositories
docs.text:
Id: 25fa2def-a118-4f60-9117-89ab50da4cf2 Type: decision Status: active Evidence: confirmed Source: ADR-001 (docs/adr/001-copier-over-cookiecutter.md) Revisit when: copier update stops being a first-class feature, or a Python-native alternative gains native template-update support

Copier renders this template. Generated projects carry a .copier-answers.yml and pull later template changes with copier update.

Reason: native update support matters most for a template that keeps evolving — adopters pull new features, CI improvements and dependency updates instead of re-applying them by hand. Conditional file inclusion via filename patterns is cleaner than hook-based approaches, the answers file makes updates reproducible, and full Jinja2 (whitespace control, raw blocks for GitHub Actions syntax) is required by the workflow templates. Copier is actively maintained and aligned with the uv/hatchling ecosystem the generated projects use.

Rejected alternative: Cookiecutter — the largest ecosystem, but no native update/sync; pulling upstream changes is manual work.

Rejected alternative: Cruft — adds cruft update/cruft check on top of Cookiecutter, but as a wrapper it is limited by Cookiecutter's internals.

Rejected alternative: Yeoman — JavaScript-based, not Python-native, heavier runtime dependency.

Rejected alternative: GitHub template repositories — no variable substitution and no conditional logic.

Consequence: adopters need copier installed; the template ecosystem is smaller than Cookiecutter's; syntax differs slightly (copier.yml).

docs.title: The worker exposes an env-injectable broker factory; lazy broker imports were rejected
docs.text:
Id: b00a3a49-7fbf-4d87-98fa-73519b994c8e Type: decision Status: active Evidence: confirmed Source: ADR-008 §1 and its implementation revision note (docs/adr/008-worker-broker-testing-strategy.md); the pattern was proven in litestar-faststream and litestar-events#9 Revisit when: a worker gains a second broker, or FastStream changes how a broker is constructed See: components.md#component-dependencies-are-core-dependencies-there-is-no-empty-all-extra — e9b25624-f621-4071-bd99-a7cde620189a — as of 2026-10-11

worker/app.py provides build_broker(url=None), which resolves the connection at call time (argument, broker-specific env var, local default) and registers the subscriber and publisher on the broker it returns; a module-level broker = build_broker() still serves the entry point. The handler and publisher are factory-local closures, so the unit test asserts on a response delivered to a collector subscriber rather than importing internals.

Reason: the original draft proposed lazy broker imports. Implementation showed that buys nothing here: there is one broker, its driver is a core runtime dependency and so always present, and the broker was constructed at module top, so the driver loads at import regardless of where the statement sits. The real blocker to integration testing was construction at import time — a localhost-bound singleton tests cannot retarget. The factory is the seam a real round-trip test needs: a fresh broker pointed at a throwaway instance, no import-order games.

Rejected alternative: lazy broker imports — the reasoning above.

Consequence: the factory returns only the broker; subscriber and publisher become closures rather than importable module globals, so tests assert on observable behaviour (a response reaching a collector subscriber), not wiring.

docs.title: Real-broker integration tests: testcontainers locally, per-broker CI mechanism
docs.text:
Id: 73e209d9-60ad-4492-9807-28192b480480 Type: decision Status: active Evidence: confirmed Source: ADR-008 §2 and its 2026-08 amendment (docs/adr/008-worker-broker-testing-strategy.md); issues #169 and #166 Revisit when: GitHub service containers can override the image command, Kafka/RabbitMQ gain a usable readiness probe, or Docker becomes available on non-Linux runners See: testing-strategy.md#the-worker-exposes-an-env-injectable-broker-factory-lazy-broker-imports-were-rejected — b00a3a49-7fbf-4d87-98fa-73519b994c8e — as of 2026-10-11 See: ci-topology.md#per-component-markers-path-filtered-jobs-and-one-coverage-gate-per-component — 467b6cc3-775b-4e4c-9a8e-b0d1c3d733ac — as of 2026-10-11

An integration-marked test round-trips a message through the real driver. It is deselected from the default suite and run by an on-demand tox env and a conditional, Ubuntu-only worker-integration CI job keyed to the one chosen broker. Container startup lives in a plain context manager: when the broker's URL env var is already set it connects directly; otherwise it starts a testcontainer. In CI, redis and nats use runner-provided services: containers (the split lives once, as the ci_service field on worker_broker_spec in copier.yml, with health_cmd: null marking "no usable in-container probe"); kafka and rabbitmq keep testcontainers. The env runs with a broad deprecation-warning demotion and a pytest timeout.

Reason: the in-memory test broker stubs out exactly the things that regress — serialization, connection handling, driver compatibility — and CI never started a broker. Docker is reliably available only on Ubuntu runners, so the cross-OS matrix must stay Docker-free. testcontainers owns the lifecycle from the test, so a laptop run matches CI. The original reasoning over-generalized against services:: for fast-starting brokers the runner starts, health-gates and injects the connection before the job, which is lighter than in-test orchestration; Kafka's advertised listeners and RabbitMQ's readiness are not worth that path. NATS runs without a health check because its monitoring endpoint needs a container command that service containers cannot set, and the test's own connect-retry covers readiness. A context manager rather than a fixture because a fixture consumed only by a deselected test reads as unused to the dead-fixtures check in style. Module-scoping the warning demotion was tried and rejected: CLI -W module matching is exact, and drivers attribute warnings via stacklevel to arbitrary caller frames.

Rejected alternative: services: for every broker — static YAML without per-test lifecycle, and Kafka/RabbitMQ readiness is not worth it.

Rejected alternative: a fan-out over all four brokers — a generated project has exactly one.

Consequence: the integration test file is in coverage omit, since it is collected but deselected in the default suite. The larger runtime integration of FastStream inside the Litestar app is explicitly out of scope.

docs.title: Coverage exclusions are per-site pragmas, and the globs must match the installed layout
docs.text:
